description:
Desktop app for Windows that applies performance, privacy, gaming and maintenance tweaks with automatic one-click rollback.

PC Tweaker applies real Windows system tweaks (registry, power plan, network DNS, temp file cleanup) across Performance, Privacy, Gaming and Maintenance categories. Every change saves a snapshot of the previous value before it's applied, so any tweak can be reverted with one click. Also reads live hardware temperatures, load and power draw, inventories installed drivers, and includes in-app auto-update.
PC Tweaker 1.8.0
Windows can now repair itself from here, cookies survive a cleanup, and the startup list finally shows everything that actually starts.
Windows integrity check and repair
DISM and SFC — the tools Microsoft support asks people to run from a command prompt — with a progress bar and a plain verdict. The check is free; the repair sequence and the WinSxS shrink are Pro.
DISM is forced to /English so the result is read from a sentence that does not change with your display language, and when it cannot be read confidently the app says "finished, here is the log" rather than inventing a clean bill of health. The repair runs DISM /RestoreHealth before sfc /scannow, in that order, because SFC repairs system files from the component store — running it first against a corrupt store just fails slowly. /ResetBase is deliberately not offered: it permanently discards the ability to uninstall updates already installed.
Selective cookie cleaning
The browser cleaner deletes the whole cookie file, which signs you out of everything — which is why most people click it once and never again.
This removes tracking and advertising cookies while keeping the ones holding a sign-in, against an editable keep-list that covers subdomains: adding google.com also keeps accounts.google.com. Scanning works while the browser is open; cleaning needs it closed, because writing to a database a running Chromium holds corrupts its next write. The database is copied first, so a clean can be undone.
Third-party app caches
Shader caches, game launchers, chat apps and package managers sit on gigabytes they rebuild on their own. Thirteen hand-verified targets — DirectX, NVIDIA, AMD and Intel shader caches, Steam, Epic, Battle.net, Discord, VS Code, npm, pip, crash dumps and Windows error reports — every one checked against a single rule: deleting it costs time, never data.
These are deleted for good rather than recycled, and the app says so: sending fifteen gigabytes to the Recycle Bin frees nothing until the bin is emptied. Scanning is free.
The startup list was missing half of what starts
As a 64-bit process the app only ever read the 64-bit registry view, so every entry belonging to 32-bit software — most consumer installers — was invisible on a screen whose entire job is to be complete. It now covers the 32-bit Run key and the Startup folder as well, each toggled through the approval key Windows itself writes, so what you see here still matches Task Manager.
Scheduled startup tasks
Software updaters moved out of the Run key and into the Task Scheduler years ago, precisely because nothing surfaces them there. Third-party logon and boot tasks are now listed and switchable. Windows' own tasks are not listed at all, and their state is read from each task's XML rather than from a status word that changes with your display language.
Also in this release
- Game Sessions frees memory on launch. Starting a registered game now also asks Windows to page out everything else's working set, and reports how much came back.
- Lifetime has a card of its own. The Lifetime tab used to show a plan labelled "Pro" beside a Free column nobody arrived for. It now says what buying outright uniquely gives you.
- Every button shows a hand cursor again. Tailwind v4 ships cursor: default on buttons where v3 left the browser's pointer alone, and the whole interface had quietly inherited it.
Every change is still snapshotted before it is applied and revertible individually or all at once. Anything needing administrator rights asks for a UAC prompt only for that action — the app itself always runs unprivileged.
